claims.text: A dense network of nanoscale grain boundaries is a primary governor of high-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys.
Severe lattice distortion acts together with nanoscale grain boundaries to produce exceptional stability.
The grain-boundary network provides abundant defect sinks.
The combined grain-boundary network and lattice distortion slow diffusion-driven segregation and precipitation.
The proposed starting material is a nanocrystalline BCC or FCC high-entropy solid solution with a statistically homogeneous elemental distribution.
Grain-boundary elemental segregation can modify local short-range order.
Nanoscale grain boundaries hinder grain growth.
Nanoscale grain boundaries enhance interstitial-vacancy recombination.
Severe lattice distortion in a random multielement solid solution retards atomic diffusion.
Retarded atomic diffusion suppresses phase separation and secondary-phase nucleation.
The proposed grain-boundary and lattice-distortion mechanisms jointly slow coarsening, precipitation, and chemical segregation.
After identical high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will undergo less grain growth than a lower-entropy nanocrystalline comparator.
After identical high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will form deleterious precipitates more slowly or not at all relative to the comparator.
After identical high-temperature exposure, the high-entropy nanoalloy will retain greater chemical homogeneity than the comparator.
The prediction applies over approximately 750–1173 K when processing has produced a stable nanostructure.
Material systems produced by substantially different processing routes or thermal histories may deviate from the prediction.
A five-or-more-component equiatomic alloy necessarily has high lattice distortion.
Annealing at 1173 K for 30 minutes is a feasible high-temperature test condition for a refractory high-entropy nanoalloy.
